traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Assuming Indika is a primary source; it is actually known through fragments in later works.
Confusing Ashoka's Puranic mentions with contemporary Mauryan literary evidence.
Over-reliance on Arthashastra as a literal account of reality; it is a normative (prescriptive) text, not descriptive.

sections.title: 1. Core Study Notes
sections.content:
Secular Sources

  • Arthashastra (Kautilya)
  • Indika (Megasthenes)
  • Mudrarakshasa (Vishakhadatta)

Religious Sources

  • Buddhist: Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa
  • Jain: Parishishtaparvan
  • Puranic: Dynastic lists

Core Literary Categorization

  • Arthashastra: Focuses on Saptanga theory, espionage, and taxation.
  • Indika: Describes the 7-fold caste system and administrative city committees.
  • Mudrarakshasa: Dramatizes the struggle of Chanakya against the Nandas to install Chandragupta.
SourceAuthorKey Contribution
ArthashastraKautilyaPolitical science & Administration
IndikaMegasthenesSocial structure & Geography
MudrarakshasaVishakhadattaHistorical political drama

practiceQuestions.q: Who among the following is the author of the ancient Indian treatise 'Arthashastra'?
practiceQuestions.sol: Kautilya, also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta, was the chief minister and mentor of Chandragupta Maurya and authored the Arthashastra, a fundamental text on statecraft, economy, and military strategy. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part I]

practiceQuestions.q: Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador who wrote 'Indica', was sent to the court of which Mauryan ruler?
practiceQuestions.sol: Megasthenes was an ambassador of Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya at Pataliputra. His accounts survive in fragments in the works of later Greek writers. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which Buddhist text provides extensive accounts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka and his conversion to Buddhism?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Mahavamsa (along with Dipavamsa), the Sri Lankan Chronicle, provides crucial historical narrative on Ashoka, his relationship with the Sangha, and the dispatch of missions to spread Buddhism. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part I]

practiceQuestions.q: The play 'Mudrarakshasa', which details how Chanakya maneuvered Chandragupta to the throne, was written by whom?
practiceQuestions.sol: Mudrarakshasa is a Sanskrit drama written by Vishakhadatta belonging to the Gupta period that vividly describes political intrigues of Chanakya against Rakshasa, the minister of the Nandas. [Primary Reference: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: In Kautilya's Arthashastra, the term 'Sita' refers to which of the following?
practiceQuestions.sol: According to the Arthashastra, 'Sita' denotes revenue derived from crown lands, which were directly cultivated under the supervision of the Sitadhyaksha (superintendent of agriculture). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following Jain texts contains accounts relating to Chandragupta Maurya spending his last days in Sravanabelagola?
practiceQuestions.sol: Bhadrabahu Charita and other Jain traditions record that Chandragupta Maurya abdicated his throne, became a Jain monk under Bhadrabahu, and migrated to Karnataka where he performed Sallekhana. [Primary Reference: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: The Puranas mention the Mauryan dynasty immediately after which ruling dynasty?
practiceQuestions.sol: Puranic literature (such as the Vayu Purana and Matsya Purana) provides dynastic lists noting that Chandragupta Maurya, aided by Kautilya, overthrew the last Nanda king. [Primary Reference: Pargiter, The Purana Text of the Dynasties of the Kali Age]

practiceQuestions.q: In the administrative vocabulary of the Arthashastra, 'Samaharta' refers to:
opts: Chief justice of the supreme court
practiceQuestions.sol: The Samaharta was responsible for the collection of revenue from all sources across the Mauryan empire (revenue administration), while the Sannidhata was the chief treasurer. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: Which classical Greek author wrote the comprehensive historical narrative 'Anabasis of Alexander' and mentioned details of Indian polity prior to Maurya?
practiceQuestions.sol: Arrian wrote 'Anabasis' based on contemporary accounts of Alexander's campaign, which serves as a vital backdrop to the political condition of India on the eve of the rise of the Mauryas. [Primary Reference: R.C. Majumdar, The Classical Accounts of India]

practiceQuestions.q: According to Megasthenes' Indica, the municipal administration of Pataliputra was divided into how many boards of five members each?
practiceQuestions.sol: Megasthenes noted that Pataliputra's city administration was managed by a city council of 30 members, divided into six committees or boards of five members each, overseeing industries, foreigners, births/deaths, trade, manufacturing, and tax collection. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part I]

practiceQuestions.q: How does Kautilya's Arthashastra characterize the nature of the Mauryan state compared to Megasthenes' account of Indian society?
opts: Arthashastra presents a decentralized tribal federation, while Megasthenes describes an absolute theocracy.

Arthashastra outlines an intensely bureaucratic, interventionist state, whereas Megasthenes highlights a uniquely prosperous society divided into seven occupational classes without recognizing the traditional varna system.
Both sources completely ignore economic activities and focus strictly on military campaigns.
Arthashastra advocates laissez-faire economics, whereas Megasthenes describes complete state monopoly over all lands.
practiceQuestions.sol: Kautilya's Arthashastra details an interventionist state controlling mines, commerce, agriculture, and espionage. Conversely, Megasthenes observed Indian society through Greek eyes, famously categorizing population into seven endogamous occupational groups rather than the classical four varnas. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300]

practiceQuestions.q: Analyze the concept of 'Kantashodhana' in the judicial system outlined within the Arthashastra.
opts: Civil courts dealing with land disputes, inheritance, and marriage contracts.
Criminal courts aimed at suppressing anti-social elements, crime, and eliminating thorns (criminals/corrupt officials) from society.
Religious tribunals run exclusively by Buddhist monks for moral transgressions.
Military tribunals handling cases of treason among foreign mercenaries.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Arthashastra categorizes courts into Dharmasthiya (civil courts) and Kantashodhana (criminal courts). Kantashodhana courts were presided over by three commissioners to check crimes, corruption, and social malpractices. [Primary Reference: R.S. Sharma, Aspects of Political Ideas and Institutions in Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: How do Buddhist literary sources like the Ashokavadana portray the transition of Ashoka from 'Chandasoka' to 'Dharmasoka'?
opts: As an economic transformation caused by heavy taxation and agricultural collapse.
As a spiritual and moral awakening triggered by remorse over the bloodshed of the Kalinga war, guided by Buddhist teachings.
As a political strategy forced upon him by a rebellion of Greek satraps in the northwest.
As a surrender of imperial power to the Ajivika ascetics.
practiceQuestions.sol: Literary texts like Ashokavadana and Dipavamsa capture the psychological and ideological shift in Ashoka's governance philosophy, moving from military conquest (Digvijaya) to moral conquest (Dhammavijaya) post-Kalinga. [Primary Reference: John S. Strong, The Legend of King Ashoka]

practiceQuestions.q: Which literary text provides detailed references to the employment of a widespread espionage network consisting of 'Gudhapurushas' (secret agents) in Mauryan administration?
practiceQuestions.sol: Kautilya's Arthashastra outlines a sophisticated intelligence machinery comprising stationary (Sanstha) and wandering (Sanchara) spies to monitor state officials, citizens, and foreign entities. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: What does the absence of slavery in Megasthenes' Indica signify regarding Greek versus Indian socio-economic observations?
opts: Slavery did not exist in any form in ancient India.
Megasthenes failed to recognize chattel slavery because Indian agrarian labor conditions (such as 'Dasas' and 'Karmakaras' in Arthashastra) differed significantly from the Greek slave-owning economy.
Megasthenes was banned from interacting with the laboring classes by the Mauryan court.
Slaves in India held higher political office than free citizens.
practiceQuestions.sol: Megasthenes stated that 'all Indians are free and no Indian is a slave'. However, Indian texts like Arthashastra clearly mention dasas (slaves) employed in domestic and economic tasks, indicating that Megasthenes missed the specific nature of Indian bondage compared to classical Greco-Roman chattel slavery. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas]

practiceQuestions.q: Which text provides the earliest literary reference to the Mauryan coinage system and the testing of coins by the 'Ruparakshika'?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Arthashastra provides extensive details on the minting of punch-marked silver coins (Panas) and copper coins, with the 'Lakshanakshaksha' inspecting minting and 'Ruparakshika' testing currency for circulation in the market. [Primary Reference: D.N. Jha, Ancient India in Historical Outline]

practiceQuestions.q: How do classical Greek accounts describe the military strength of the Nanda and Mauryan empires in terms of infantry, cavalry, chariots, and elephants?
opts: They mention negligible military forces relying entirely on mercenaries.
They record colossal standing armies, with war elephants forming the core striking force, corroborated by Arthashastra's mention of a six-member war office.
They emphasize naval dominance across the Indian Ocean.
They state that Mauryans completely abolished chariots and cavalry.
practiceQuestions.sol: Plutarch, Diodorus, and Curtius note the massive military size of the Gangaridai and Prasii (Nanda/Maurya), featuring hundreds of thousands of infantry, tens of thousands of cavalry, chariots, and thousands of war elephants. This matches Megasthenes' account of the six military boards. [Primary Reference: R.C. Majumdar, The Classical Accounts of India]

practiceQuestions.q: What is the significance of the term 'Vishyavikas' or trade routes mentioned in Mauryan literary sources?
opts: They were exclusively meant for religious pilgrimages by Buddhist monks.
Arthashastra emphasizes royal control over both land routes (Santhapatha) and water routes (Vavipatha) to regulate commerce, taxation, and military movement.
Trade routes were uncontrolled and entirely managed by independent merchant guilds without state interference.
They connected Pataliputra exclusively to Roman ports in the Mediterranean.
practiceQuestions.sol: The Arthashastra attaches immense importance to trade routes (Vanikpatha), distinguishing between northern (Uttar पाठ) and southern routes, and advocates heavy policing and toll collection (Panyadhyaksha) to maximize state income. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q: How do Buddhist texts depict the economic policy of Emperor Ashoka following his adoption of Buddhism?
opts: Complete dismantling of the taxation system and abolition of all currency.
A shift toward ethical governance, promotion of welfare (planting trees, digging wells, medical care for humans and animals), while maintaining administrative and fiscal control.
Confiscation of all private property and transition to a monastic communal economy.
Outsourcing state revenue collection entirely to foreign merchants.
practiceQuestions.sol: While Ashoka's Edicts and Buddhist literature emphasize Dhamma, non-violence, and social welfare, the state apparatus, taxation, and economic controls established during earlier reigns remained functional to sustain the vast empire. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas]

practiceQuestions.q: What is the historical significance of the literary references found in Patanjali's 'Mahabhasya' regarding the Mauryan dynasty?
opts: It describes the birth of Chandragupta Maurya in a royal palace.
It mentions how the Maurya family amassed wealth by selling idols/images of gods ('Mauryairartharthibhirarchah prakalpitah'), reflecting economic practices.
It provides a verbatim copy of Ashoka's edicts in Sanskrit.
It records the exact date of the assassination of Brihadratha, the last Mauryan king.
practiceQuestions.sol: Patanjali's Mahabhasya refers to the Mauryas as being greedy for wealth and setting up images of gods for worship to generate income ('Archah prakalpitah'). This provides a rare non-Buddhist, critical literary insight into Mauryan revenue-generation methods. [Primary Reference: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Kautilya's Arthashastra:
1. It is divided into 15 adhikaranas (books) and deals exclusively with military strategy and warfare.
2. It recognizes seven constituent elements of the state (Saptanga theory), wherein the king (Swamin) is placed at the apex.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because while Arthashastra covers military strategy (Book 10), it is a comprehensive treatise covering civil law, taxation, agriculture, mining, trade, diplomacy, and administration across its 15 books, not exclusively warfare. Statement 2 is correct; it details the Saptanga theory (Swamin, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Bala, Mitra). [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part I]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Megasthenes' account of Mauryan society:
1. Megasthenes explicitly mentioned the existence of the caste system (four varnas) and untouchability in Pataliputra.
2. He noted that Indian society was divided into seven distinct occupational classes, including philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers, and councillors.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because Megasthenes did not understand or mention the traditional varna or caste system; instead, he misconstrued endogamous professions as castes. Statement 2 is correct; he famously classified Indian society into seven hereditary occupational categories. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Early India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Mauryan taxation as per literary evidence:
1. 'Bhaga' was the main land revenue tax levied on agricultural produce, typically fixed at one-sixth to one-fourth of the produce.
2. 'Pranaya' was an emergency tax levied by the state during times of financial crisis or war.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Bhaga was the regular agricultural tax (usually 1/6th), and Pranaya (meaning 'gift of affection', ironically) was a forced emergency levy collected by the Mauryan state when treasuries fell short during crises, as detailed in the Arthashastra. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Buddhist and Jain accounts of the Mauryan Empire:
1. Buddhist texts like Mahavamsa portray Ashoka as a ruthless tyrant before his conversion, whereas Jain accounts credit Chandragupta Maurya with patronizing Jainism.
2. Both Buddhist and Jain texts completely omit any mention of Kautilya in the rise of the Mauryan empire.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; Buddhist chronicles emphasize Ashoka's transition from 'Chandasoka' to 'Dharmasoka', and Jain texts (like Parishishtaparvan) link Chandragupta to Bhadrabahu and Jainism. Statement 2 is incorrect because Jain texts such as Hemachandra's Parishishtaparvan explicitly mention Chanakya (Kautilya) and his role in placing Chandragupta on the throne. [Primary Reference: Upinder Singh, A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial and administrative officials mentioned in the Arthashastra:
1. 'Pradeshtri' functioned as executive officers cum magistrates responsible for tracking criminals under the Kantashodhana courts.
2. 'Nagarikadhyaksha' was the superintendent of the mint responsible for issuing silver and gold currency.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; Pradeshtris were police-cum-magistrates operating under Kantashodhana. Statement 2 is incorrect because Nagaradhyaksha (or Nagarikadhyaksha) was the superintendent of the city (Pataliputra/urban administration), whereas the superintendent of the mint was the 'Lakshanakshaksha' or 'Swarnadhyaksha'. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Ancient India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding foreign accounts of the Mauryan period:
1. Justin described Chandragupta Maurya as a man of humble origin who was born of a Shudra woman named Mura.
2. Strabo and Arrian noted that slavery, as practiced in Greece, was strictly absent in India based on accounts of Megasthenes.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Roman historian Justin referred to Chandragupta as being of humble birth (and etymologically linked 'Maurya' to Mura). Greek writers like Strabo, Arrian, and Diodorus echoed Megasthenes' observation that Indians do not use slaves. [Primary Reference: R.C. Majumdar, The Classical Accounts of India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic role of the state according to the Arthashastra:
1. The Mauryan state maintained monopolies over vital sectors such as mining (Akshadhyaksha), salt manufacture (Lavanadhyaksha), and liquor production (Suradhyaksha).
2. Private trade was completely prohibited, and all commercial exchange was conducted directly through state-owned cooperative stores.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; the Arthashastra details extensive state control and departmental superintendents (Adhyakshas) over mines, salt, and liquor. Statement 2 is incorrect because private trade and merchant guilds (Srenis) coexisted alongside state-run enterprises; private merchants operated under state licenses and paid heavy duties. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Early India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the literary accounts of Mauryan provincial administration:
1. The Arthashastra mentions the division of the empire into provinces governed by royal princes (Kumaras or Aryaputras).
2. The provinces were further subdivided into districts (Ahars or Vishayas) administered by officials like 'Pradeshtris' and 'Rajjukas'.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Provincial and district-level administrative units (districts under Sthanikas and Gopas, revenue/justice under Rajjukas) find extensive mention in both Mauryan epigraphy (Ashokan Edicts) and administrative manuals like the Arthashastra. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Themes in Indian History Part I]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the transmission and discovery of Kautilya's Arthashastra:
1. The text was lost for centuries and was rediscovered and published in 1905 by R. Shamasastry.
2. The language of the Arthashastra is classical Sanskrit, written in a mix of prose (sutra) and verse (shloka) styles.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. R. Shamasastry discovered a complete palm-leaf manuscript of the Arthashastra in the Oriental Research Institute Mysore in 1904 and published it in 1909 (with preliminary announcements/translations starting around 1905). The text is composed in prose and verse in classical Sanskrit. [Primary Reference: R. Shamasastry, Kautilya's Arthashastra - Introduction]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the social conditions depicted in the Arthashastra:
1. It permits widow remarriage (Punarbhu) and outlines legal frameworks for divorce under specific circumstances.
2. It explicitly prohibits women from participating in economic production or engaging in independent trade.
Which of the statements given below is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; the Arthashastra provides detailed civil laws regarding marriage, property rights of women (Stridhana), widow remarriage, and valid grounds for divorce (moksha). Statement 2 is incorrect because the Arthashastra mentions female artisans, weavers (working in state textile factories under Sutradhyaksha), and independent businesswomen participating in economic life. [Primary Reference: Romila Thapar, Early India]
